display.title: Why We Shake When We Daven: The Rebbe Rashab's Test
display.summary_short: Young Yosef Yitzchak trains a non-Jewish boy to read Ashrei exactly like his Jewish friend, but his father, the Rebbe Rashab, still knows which boy is Jewish, and explains why.
display.summary_long: Uncle Yossi begins with the lulav: we shake it in six directions to show that Hashem protects us from every side. Shaking is a sign of life, and shuckling is even a sign of a Jew. The story: young Yosef Yitzchak, the only son of the Rebbe Rashab and later the Frierdiker Rebbe, is allowed to sit in on his father's farbrengens and writes down everything he hears. Once he hears his father say that a Jew's body, not only his soul, is holy, so that he can tell a Jew just by looking at him. Curious, the boy sets up a test. He teaches a polite non-Jewish neighbor boy, word by word, to recite the opening lines of Ashrei perfectly, has a Jewish friend learn the same lines, and dresses the two alike. His father asks each to read from a siddur and then quietly tells his son which boy is Jewish. The amazed boy asks how. The Rebbe Rashab explains that at Matan Torah the people saw and trembled, and that trembling before Hashem was handed down to every generation. The Jewish boy swayed as he read; that is the mark of a Jew who stood at Har Sinai.
display.lesson: Shaking when we daven is our inheritance from Har Sinai, where every Jewish soul trembled before Hashem.

date.note: Date of the episode 531 airing; the story also aired in episode 310.

'The people saw and trembled' at Matan Torah.
